claims.text: The stability of equimolar HEA nanoparticles from 473 to 1923 K is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and thermally activated elemental diffusion.
High configurational entropy favors a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Thermal activation of elemental diffusion competes with solid-solution stability.
Mixing enthalpy influences the formation of equimolar single-phase HEAs.
Sufficiently negative mixing enthalpy combined with high diffusion barriers suppresses segregation and phase separation under reactive catalytic conditions.
Preservation of crystal structure and surface chemistry is required for optimal catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Equimolar or near-equimolar quinary nanoparticles can initially be crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Elemental diffusion and surface segregation are mediated by mixing enthalpy and element-specific diffusion activation barriers.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous solid solution.
When thermal energy becomes comparable to or exceeds an element's diffusion barrier, that element can migrate and segregate.
Surface reactivity in catalytic environments may accelerate segregation or promote intermetallic-phase formation.
Under inert thermoelectric operating conditions, bulk lattice stability is challenged mainly by thermally activated diffusion.
HEA nanoparticles with strongly negative mixing enthalpies and high diffusion barriers will retain a single solid-solution phase with minimal segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Surface segregation or new-phase formation under catalytic conditions will measurably degrade catalytic activity relative to the initial baseline.
Structural stability under inert conditions will produce minimal changes in electrical and thermal transport properties relative to baseline.
The proposed comparison controls initial composition and structure while varying reactive versus inert atmosphere during stepwise heating from 473 to 1923 K.
The stability prediction holds only while thermal energy is insufficient to overcome key diffusion barriers and the environment does not strongly promote surface reactions.
Temperatures near 1923 K or highly reactive gas atmospheres may cause phase separation or substantial elemental segregation.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states only that a catalytic atmosphere may accelerate segregation, so it permits no detectable difference between reactive and inert groups. The falsification rule nevertheless treats the absence of a difference as falsifying, making that rule stronger than the stated prediction.
